description: Mr. Moore is a recurring figure who visits the Exchange to speak with his uncle Wight, expresses concern about news and dirt in his household, and spends time at Whitehall and Westminster Hall. He meets the narrator at various points, including at the Exchange and at Whitehall, where he informs the narrator that the next day is a Seal day and that they must wait upon Lord Roberts, Lord Privy Seal. At Whitehall, the Lord Privy Seal receives the narrator and Mr. Moore, who reads bills as customary; the meeting ends well. Mr. Moore also visits his father, drinks at the Samson in Paul's Churchyard, and purchases green say for curtains. He is troubled by his neglect of current events and the state of his home. The narrator, meanwhile, attends the Exchange, the Theatre, and Whitehall, where he learns of Lady Sandwich’s childbirth and meets the Lord Privy Seal after a morning absence.

The narrator frequently visits his father's house and mother, where he observes growing discontent, particularly in his mother's demeanor, which has become simple and unquiet. He discusses financial matters with Sir Robert Bernard, learning that a sum of L164 due to them will be included with debts to the heir at law, a situation that deeply saddens him. He meets Tom Trice, who has come with his father to Goody Gorum's, and later visits Tom Trice’s alehouse with Dr. Williams to examine and sign a copy of the uncle’s will, which Tom filed a caveat on in support of his mother. The narrator also spends time with friends, dines with Lady Digby, and attends social events, including a visit to the Vineyard and a performance of 'Brenoralt,' which he finds poorly acted. He worries about financial instability and emotional entanglements, especially regarding his wife’s brother Balty, and fears being tied to others again. The family receives news that Tom Trice’s actions have caused concern, and the narrator ultimately feels relief after the will is probated.

The narrator engages in various business activities throughout the day, including attending meetings in the afternoon and evening, and discussing land purchases with his father regarding his uncle Robert, offering L600 ready money and L150 per annum, though only having L500 ready. His aunt sends a letter stating the uncle is unwell, prompting the father to visit him. In the afternoon, the narrator meets Old William Luffe, who pays L20 and acknowledges the surrender of Sturtlow to him. On another day, Mr. Holden sends a beaver costing L4 5s, which later becomes a point of concern when a hat is left as a substitute. The narrator also attends a play, stays at Sir W. Batten’s, and spends time in the garden with Sir W. Pen, playing flageolette and drinking claret until 12 at night. After a cold day in London, he buys coarse woollen stockings. The narrator agrees with his aunt that she will quit the house in exchange for L10, and all matters beyond that are left to law, which pleases everyone.

The Privy Seal holds a document from the Lord Chancellor, who obtained large grants of lands and manors from the king, including a warrant in his own handwriting authorizing Sir Stephen Fox to pay L20,000—equivalent to 10 million dollars in 2000—to the Chancellor, a sum not noticed by anyone. This money was used to clear a mortgage on Clarendon Park, and part of it was believed to come from France via the sale of Dunkirk. Mons. Eschar waited at the Privy Seal for a warrant of L5,000 for My Lord of Sandwich’s preparation for Portugal. The narrator visited La Belle Pierce, who was pregnant, and stayed with her and Mrs. Clifford, enjoying merriment. At a tavern near the Savoy, Mons. Eschar strongly criticized English music and praised French music, which angered the narrator, leading him to leave. The speaker met his wife at the Wardrobe, which was My Lord of Sandwich’s birthday celebration, where they had friends present. A woman with a rod kept time to the musique.

The narrator interacts with Ned Pickering in St. James's Park, where Pickering complains about the lewdness and beggary of the Court, prompting the narrator to express regret and fear of further ruin. They later dine at the Wardrobe, attend the Opera to see "The Witts" (which the narrator enjoys), and go to the Devil tavern with Captain Ferrers, returning home by coach. The narrator is troubled by his inability to focus on business and is drawn to plays. A vessel sent with goods from my Lord to Lynn is reported to have arrived in Soale Bay, though its purpose is unclear. The narrator also attends the Theatre with Holcroft, his father, and brother Tom, discussing the honourability of a naval career, and later sees "Harry the 4th." He visits Worcester House, where the King arrives in plain attire, and goes with Mr. Moore to Chelsy, where they meet the Lord Privy Seal, examine and seal a document, and walk home after losing their coach. The narrator also spends time with his father, discusses cloth business, and gives his wife L4 for lace and personal items.

On the 16th, the narrator and their father organized affairs, allowed the crop to grow, and appointed Stankes as their bayly, while Falconer of Woolwich attended the Privy Seal, dined with his father and children, and met Dr. John Williams, who was well informed about Gravely. A widespread fever, rare and previously only seen during plague times, killed Tom Fuller, Dr. Nichols, and Tom Whitton, and left Lord General Monk dangerously ill. On the 18th, the narrator visited Captain Lambert, admired his wife’s needleworks, and met Jack Cole, with whom they shared good humour. On the 19th, the narrator saw his stairs finished by painters, attended the office, and was sent for by My Lady Sandwich to dine with her at her father’s house. The narrator also went to White Hall, where they learned Lord General Monk remained very ill, and visited La Belle Pierce and St. James’s Park. Mr. Moore advised the speaker about the will, noting its witnesses were all legatees, and gave the narrator a copy of Hooker’s Ecclesiastical Polity to read.

The Court is in poor condition due to emulacion, poverty, drinking, swearing, and loose amours, leading to widespread confusion and public discontent, especially over the Clergy's high status and the inadequate Benevolence, which amounts to L33,743 and was established on May 31st, 1661. The Office faces financial difficulties, with bills sold at a 10 per cent loss, and is attempting to acquire Sir R. Ford's house but is hindered by ownership division and a personal obligation to pay L200 per annum, making acquisition unlikely. The Comptroller invites the narrator to view houses near the office, but the plan is abandoned as the houses do not appeal. On Midsummer-day, the narrator visits his father’s completed and neat house, where he meets his cozen J. On the 24th, Captain Holmes brings a large baboon from Guiny, which resembles a man, understands English, and the narrator believes it may be a monster born from a man and a she-baboon, possibly teachable to speak or make signs. The season is marked by widespread fatal fevers.

The narrator interacts with various figures, including Lord Crew, who favors him and his lady, and visits the Devil tavern, Uncle Fenner’s, and the Crane tavern. On the 22nd, he dines with Lord Crew, attends a performance of Ben Jonson’s comedy *The Alchymist* (first printed in 1612), and meets Little Luellin and Blirton, who take him to Mr. Hodges in Lincoln’s Inn Fields, where they drink Rhenish wine and are merry. The narrator sups with his Lady, who consults about Lord Hinchinabroke’s illness and plans to send her sons Sidney, Oliver, and John to his house to avoid smallpox. The narrator is troubled by both Lord Hinchinabroke’s and Lord Sandwich’s illnesses; Lord Sandwich, who was ill in Alicante and twice let blood, writes a letter dated 22nd July last confirming his sickness, though he is now recovering. A woman born in Portugal in 1638 married Charles II in 1662, later became Regent in Portugal in 1704, and died in 1705.

The narrator, along with his wife, attended the Theatre to see 'The Joviall Crew', where the King, Duke, Duchess, and Madame Palmer were present, and the narrator's wife enjoyed seeing them throughout the play, which was full of mirth. On the 26th, the narrator met Mr. Hill of Cambridge, who served wine and claimed the state of England's Church had changed, asserting the King must favor Presbytery or the City would leave him; the narrator dismissed these claims but noted Parliament was in great disorder. The narrator had vowed to drink no wine during the week but broke the vow that day, feeling troubled and hoping God would forgive him. On the 27th, the narrator took leave of my Lord Hinchingbroke and his brother, who left for Rye and France, and discussed concerns about Mr. Edward Montagu's disposal of L5000 for the Lord's departure. The narrator also dined with his family and attended a comedy, 'Fayre Botelers', first printed in 1608 and falsely attributed to Shakespeare and Drayton. A play, 'Antipodes', was seen later and was full of mirth but contained no great matter.

The narrator is troubled by the estate's poor condition, as papers are confused and copyhold surrenders are missing, leading to land going to heir at law instead of the family. He fears his brother Tom, who manages the family trade, will fail due to lack of intelligence and care. On the 29th, Tom dines with the narrator and they discuss trade, with Tom stating he will not set up the trade elsewhere unless the father gives up profit from the London house. The narrator, under financial strain from no income and heavy borrowing, is working to correct his neglect of business duties. On the 30th, the narrator meets his father at Holborn, where they part ways, with the father traveling to Brampton to settle affairs for his mother’s arrival. The narrator also discusses Tom’s potential marriage with Mr. Evans’s daughter, but the father opposes giving away the estate, citing only a trade and house as current possession.

The narrator, suffering from a headache due to the previous night's debauch, traveled by water to Greenwich with Captain Lambert, who answered questions about ships. They ate, drank, and heard music at the Globe, where the narrator observed a woman with a rod keeping time to music, which he found simple. They visited Captain Lambert’s handsome and neat house with a fine view, then went to Bridewell to see Mr. Holland, where the narrator paid Mrs. Holland and noted that ignorant people praised a young woman who played the viallin. The weather was very hot, and the narrator removed his wastecoat. Later, the narrator visited Mr. Edward Montagu at Whitehall, where he found Montagu and his family, and sent a ship and a triangle virginall to the house by the Lord’s order. The narrator also traveled to Woolwich, drank wine and beer at a tavern, and returned home after various stops, eventually going to bed.

Samuel Pepys was a prominent figure in 17th-century England, serving as MP for Cambridge and Recorder of Cambridge until 1660. He frequently traveled to Cambridge, Deptford, and Woolwich for official duties, including inspecting ships and securing imprests for voyages. On August 1, 1661, he visited Walthamstow with Sir Williams, his wife, and Mrs. Margarett Pen, where he gave six silver spoons (excluding the porringer) to Mrs. Browne and ate a venison pasty brought from London. He later attempted to reconcile a dispute involving Lady Batten and her husband, believing the story that she left her estate to him to be true. In July 1661, he purchased a chest of drawers and an Indian gown. On August 2, he rode to Ware and conversed with a Quaker fellmonger who claimed to have been wicked all his life but changed his behavior within the last two years. Pepys was also involved in office work, including managing funds for Lord Braybrooke and Mr. Creed. He was prone to colds and wore a cloth over his belly in hot weather. A man was to go to Algier to organize the fleet and return to Lisbon.

Roger Pepys, a sober and respected figure, is described by the narrator as now honored more than ever, particularly for criticizing the young men in Parliament for poorly carrying out their duties by opposing serious initiatives. The narrator visits Cambridge, where he finds his brother John in bed at eight o'clock, which annoys him, and attends King’s College Chapel, where scholars in surplices attend service with organs. He later meets Dr. Fairbrother and spends time at the Rose Tavern with Mr. Turner and his wife, and with Mr. Sanchy and others, enjoying merriment. On the 15th, he rides to Impington and meets his uncle Talbot Pepys, who is seventy-eight, born in 1583, educated at Trinity Hall, called to the bar at the Middle Temple in 1605, and a Member of Parliament. The narrator also attends a plain sermon led by a parson who begins with “Right worshipfull and dearly beloved,” and later discusses public matters with Roger Pepys at a church service and dinner. The narrator attends Sir William Davenant’s Opera, where the second part of *The Siege of Rhodes* is performed, and the eunuch is hissed off stage despite the rest being well acted.

Townsend and his wife frequently attended church on Lord's Day, including on the 28th and 30th, where Mrs. Ramsay visited and dined with them, being welcomed. They shared a venison pasty after dinner and visited ships and showed them to guests, including Lady Jem and Pall, who had recently seen the house alone. Townsend and his wife returned home by coach and wrote a letter to his father at Brampton, who has not been heard from since Townsend left. Townsend expressed intent to join the speaker and Mr. Moore in a business venture, placing confidence in someone, and promised to assist with Mr. Young’s position in the Wardrobe if available. On the 28th, after church, they returned for dinner. The trade of briefs, a Sunday practice at St. Olave's Church, was abolished in 1828 after being levied for St. Dunstan in the West following a fire.

My Lord Hinchingbroke fell ill on the 12th, with his illness reportedly caused by fruit given to him at the narrator's house. He was in great fear of smallpox and was very ill when visited by the narrator. Mr. George Montagu advised the speaker about a ship to carry Hinchingbroke and other young gentlemen to France, noting they would travel in a hired vessel from Rye, not a man-of-war. Montagu stated that the Lord Chancellor is envied by many great men, including the Duke of Buckingham and my Lord of Bristoll, but believes he cannot be undermined due to the King's dependence on him, despite the King not loving him as a companion. A burial occurred on a Sunday afternoon, attended by many, causing disorder; Mr. Turner delivered a funeral sermon highlighting honesty, which was sufficient to make a good sermon. The Bishops were unable to keep a fast due to weather, observing it as both a fast and a feast.

The narrator travels through London, Huntingdon, and Brampton, encountering rain, which causes concern for famine and delays travel. In London, a general fast is declared on the 12th and 19th of June to avert sickness, dearth, and scarcity caused by late immoderate rain, with prayers held for a blessed change in weather and comfort, and a blessing upon the High Court of Parliament. The Lords tax themselves for the poor, with an earl paying 30s and a baron 20s; those absent from prayers pay a forfeit. The narrator spends time with Greatorex, discussing mathematics, and is concerned about rain affecting the voyage. At Huntingdon, the narrator stays with Mr. Phillips and Tom Trice, drinks heavily, and returns home to his father, who notices his drinking for the first time. The narrator visits church in London, where Quakers are noted as growing. He later attends the Wardrobe, where his Lord discusses succession with Mr. Townsend and intends to join him. The narrator also meets Mrs. Whately about a potential match, with a deposit of L200 offered.

The narrator and their father visit Mr. Rawlinson’s, where uncle Thomas arrives with two sons and uncle Wight, who is appointed by them, and the will is read. The narrator expresses thoughts on kindness to uncle Thomas, who promises to withdraw his caveat and appears content. Later, the narrator returns home to find the Lady’s three sons, glad they can assist the Lady and her Lord, though troubled by Lord of Sandwich’s health. Uncle Robert is reported to be ill with dizziness, prompting the father to go to Brampton, where he learns Robert has died. The narrator visits uncle Wight at the Mitre, where Wight is upset about the father’s absence, and later visits his aunt, who is ill. Pall is a source of distress; the narrator and Mills both decide not to keep her, with Mills convincing his father to allow her to go to the country to be observed. Pall stays with Mills’ mother and father, and after a night at a christening, she leaves, causing sorrow. Jane, Mills’ long-serving maid, is reconciled and goes to visit her mother. The narrator is troubled by Pall’s behavior and the health of Lord of Sandwich.

Martin rode from the Post House to Brampton, arriving by nine o’clock, where he found his father in good health. His uncle’s corpse was initially placed in the chimney on joint-stools but was moved to the yard overnight due to a smell; Martin watched it with two men and found his aunt in an unpleasant condition. On the 7th (Lord’s day), Martin and his father read the will in the garden, where his father gave him little or nothing immediately but affirmed well-provided care for the family. After reading the will, they prepared ribbands and gloves for the burial. On the 25th, the narrator received a box of papers from Brampton containing all of his uncle’s papers, which set him to work. The narrator also visited Dr. Williams on the 28th to discuss his aunt Pepys’s bond, where Dr. Williams stated they would not be forced to pay interest, though the narrator doubted this. Martin and his father expressed a desire to see the will, which they did on the 7th. The narrator, on various days, organized papers, visited Dr. Williams, and went to Will, while also reading a play and forging a letter to mock Sir W. Pen.

The narrator, a key figure in the narrative, interacts with multiple entities including MY LORD, LORD, MR. CREED, SYMONS, and L300. MY LORD, a prominent political figure, is appointed by the King as ambassador for the bringing over of Katherine of Braganza, born in 1638, who married Charles II on 21st May 1662. MY LORD instructs the narrator to lay out L300 in cloth for presents among the Turks and to go to Mr. Townsend to uncover the Wardrobe’s secrets, making the narrator deputy in his absence. Symons, the dancing master, accompanies MY LORD, visits the Swan tavern and White Hall, discusses the Bishop of Galloway’s controversial practice of admitting Roundtree (a former parson and mechanique) into orders, and meets Mr. Townsend, who agrees to share information. Mr. Creed is involved in financial transactions with Alderman Backwell, receiving payment for L300 and later being honored by MY LORD with five fully charged guns. The narrator manages logistics involving L300, including its transport and storage, and experiences mental distress over delivery plans. The narrative also includes social events such as attending Bartholomew Faire and dining with Mr. Creed and Mr. Shepley.

Sir W. Pen, Sir W. Batten, and the narrator reported to the Duke of York about the Navy’s poor financial condition, with bills offered at a 20 in 100 loss, prompting the Duke to promise to speak to the King and Council. The narrator and Sir W. Pen attended the Theatre to see *The Alchymist*, then visited Paul’s and the Dolphin, where they sat with Sir W. Batten. The narrator received a letter from Mr. Creed confirming Lord Hinchingbroke’s recovery from pain caused by wind in his right side and fever, with hope of sailing in a day or two. The narrator practiced singing, which is now their great trade, and attended to their Lady. On the 15th, the author saw *The Witts* at the Opera, which included new scenes, and later met Sir W. Pen at the Dolphin. On the 29th, Sir W. Pen and the narrator investigated ship delays at Deptford, finding them satisfactory. The narrator later dined with Mr. Chetwind, Gregory, Hartlibb, and Mr. Kipps at the Bell at the Maypole, members of their old club. The author also attended *Hamlet, Prince of Denmark*, where Betterton’s performance was praised.

On the 22nd, the narrator visited the Privy Seal, returned home at noon, took his wife by coach to his uncle Fenner's, where the house was hot and crowded, prompting him and his father and uncle Wight to go to an alehouse to cool off. They returned to church, where his father's family was in mourning and showed him honour, believed due to his father's will; the narrator stayed out of the sermon. Later, he and his wife, aunt Wight, and Pall went to her house for a supper of Westphalia ham before returning home. On the 30th, they dined with children, visited my Lady's bedside, and went to Drury Lane for a poorly performed French comedy, which left the narrator feeling sick; there, the wife met a son of my Lord Somersett, known from France, whom the narrator avoided. On the 31st, the narrator and Luellin visited a tavern and Bartholomew Fair, then went to a pitiful alehouse with whores, which the narrator strongly disapproved of and left with difficulty. He later met Ladies Jemimah and Paulina at the fair. On the 9th day, his wife wore a black silk gown laced with black gimp lace and was admired at my Lady's at the Wardrobe; the narrator left her there to visit Mr. Pierce, with whom he went afterward. The narrator also removed old papers of marital disputes from his father's house.

Samuel Pepys, the narrator, dined with my Lady, who is mourning her brother Samuel Crew, who died of spotted fever. He visited Westminster, the Wardrobe, and later met with Sir W. Batten and the Comptroller, where he sat late disputing with Mr. Mills. My Lady Batten attended the burial of Sir John Lawson’s daughter and received rings for herself and her husband. Pepys saw the play *Claracilla* at the theatre, which was well acted, though the theatre is now empty due to the Opera’s opening. He met Ladies Jemimah and Paulina, Mr. Pickering, and Madamoiselle at a fair, where they watched monkeys dance, an event he found disturbing due to its unclean nature. He gave each lady a bauble, a glass globe with hanging items, which pleased them. At home, he stayed to talk with my Lady for an hour, during which she recounted with innocence how Mrs. Crispe intended for the King to serve as godfather to a young lady in childbed, a story that moved Pepys deeply due to its simplicity and honesty. Pepys also sat before Mrs. Palmer, the King’s mistress, and was pleased by the experience. He suffered a cold from playing in the water, broke wind for relief, and ate supper. His uncle Robert Pepys of Brampton continued to have daily fits of stupefaction lasting 10 or 12 hours. Pepys expressed frustration over ignorant people praising him and was greedy to see a will, though he did not view it until the next day. He became increasingly interested in plays and spending money and looked askew at his wife for not conforming to court expectations.
